choices.text: Less than 0.5 A - the bulb has used some current
Exactly 0.5 A - current is the same all around a series loop
0 A - the current stops at the bulb

questions.feedback: That used-up answer is the one to unlearn: The bulb uses up the current. Reteach point: Current is not used up: an ammeter reads the same 0.5 amps on both sides of the bulb.
questions.misconception: The bulb uses up the current.
questions.prompt: An ammeter reads 0.5 A just before a bulb in a series circuit. What does an ammeter just after the bulb read?

questions.feedback: Scene s4 fixes this: I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 amps from Ohm's law, V = I R.
questions.prompt: Calculate the current when a 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor.

choices.text: It stays lit on its own branch
It goes out - series gives the charge only one path, and that path is broken

questions.feedback: Scene s3: series means one path, so one broken bulb kills the whole loop; parallel is the arrangement with branches.
questions.prompt: In a series circuit one bulb breaks. What happens to the other bulb?

questions.answer: Conventional current flows out of the battery's positive terminal, around the loop, and back into the negative terminal.
questions.feedback: Scene s2: follow the red markers - out of positive, around the loop, back into negative.
questions.prompt: State the direction of conventional current around a circuit, naming the battery terminals it leaves and returns to.
